column5: speech like rain on grass
column6: The commentary sets withered pasture beside the next ayah’s recitation; Moses asks that his teaching fall as rain and his speech as dew on grass, joining authoritative speech to the plant’s source of life.

column5: rain makes the earth sprout
column6: The commentary compares the pasture’s brief cycle with a preserved recitation; Isaiah says rain waters earth and makes it sprout before comparing that action to God’s effective word.

column5: word accomplishes its purpose
column6: The commentary places the withering pasture beside a word that will not be forgotten; Isaiah says the word from God’s mouth will not return empty, completing its rain-and-growth analogy with durable efficacy.

column5: seed sprouts through night and day
column6: The commentary says this ayah compresses a season into one immediate step, while Mark’s farmer sleeps and rises night and day as seed sprouts and grows by a process he does not know.

column5: stages from blade to ripe grain
column6: The commentary contrasts its single fe with a longer sequence of growth and drying; Mark names successive stages from stalk to full grain before harvest, supplying a precise gradual counter-image.

column5: wicked fade like green grass
column6: The commentary turns the plant’s withering into an image for people who choose the transient world; this verse says evildoers soon wither like grass and fade like green herbs, making the moral application explicit.

column5: withered leaf carried by wind
column6: The commentary’s guthā is plant matter swept away and no longer counted; Isaiah says all wither like a leaf and their iniquities carry them away like wind, adding a moral account of that disappearance.

column5: reeds need water to grow
column6: The commentary sets floating debris against hollows that retain floodwater; Job asks whether papyrus or reeds can grow without marsh and water, making water retention a condition for plant life.

column5: green plant withers before harvest
column6: The commentary holds the green pasture within the darkened debris; Job says a plant can wither while still green and uncut, giving the color change a specific image of premature loss.

column5: root rots and blossom becomes dust
column6: The commentary develops pasture turning into useless debris and being carried off; Isaiah likens judgment to fire consuming stubble, with a rotten root and blossom rising as dust, adding a moral cause and both plant parts.

column5: celestial agent makes each blade grow
column6: The commentary assigns pasture’s emergence and drying to the same Lord; this midrash says each blade of grass has a heavenly constellation that strikes it and tells it to grow, adding an intermediary account of growth without denying divine rule.

column5: rootless growth withers in sun
column6: The commentary describes guthā as uprooted vegetation that no longer holds to soil; in the sower parable a plant springs up, is scorched by the sun, and withers because it has no root.

column5: fruitless fig tree withers at Jesus’ word
column6: The commentary frames pasture’s drying as a stage in the creator’s care; Jesus’ curse makes a leafy but fruitless fig tree wither, using plant death as a judgment sign rather than a seasonal passage.

column5: green wood contrasted with dry wood
column6: The commentary traces green pasture into dry debris; Jesus uses the difference between green and dry wood to measure the severity of coming judgment, extending the plant contrast into a warning about human fate.

column5: God gives growth after planting and watering
column6: The commentary emphasizes that the same Lord brings out pasture and transforms it; Paul distinguishes planting and watering by human workers from God giving the growth, adding a division of agency within cultivation.

column5: hay and straw among building materials
column6: The commentary links guthā to the rejected, uncounted side of selection; Paul includes hay and straw among works built on a foundation, materials that cannot endure the coming test.

column5: fire tests and burns perishable work
column6: The commentary compares transient vegetation with what lasts; Paul says each person’s work is disclosed and tested by fire, adding a judgment in which the work, rather than the person, is what burns.

column5: builder survives loss of burned work
column6: The commentary’s ğuŝâ imagery can turn people themselves into debris; Paul distinguishes the person from combustible work, saying the builder may suffer loss yet be saved, a useful limit on the analogy.

column5: patient waiting for rain and harvest
column6: The commentary contrasts the compressed fe with longer stages of plant growth; James pictures a farmer waiting patiently for the crop until the early and late rains, giving the growing season its slow human rhythm.

column5: useless vine wood becomes fuel
column6: The commentary says withered pasture remains the same plant in a changed, useless state; Ezekiel’s vine wood is worthless for craft and is cast into fire as fuel, giving the loss of usefulness a judgment image.

column5: sealed spring in an enclosed garden
column6: The commentary explicitly treats water-holding hollows as a secondary image beside floating debris; the Song’s enclosed garden and sealed spring offer a specific image of protected water, though its setting is erotic rather than a flood basin.

column5: well of living water and flowing streams
column6: The commentary contrasts what a flood carries away with water retained in hollows; the Song names a well of living water and streams, a related water-source image without the commentary’s debris or flood scene.
